claim: The whole-body synaptic connectome of a 3-day-old (72 hours post fertilisation) Platynereis dumerilii larva was reconstructed from a serial electron microscopy dataset consisting of 4846 layers of 40 nm thin sections.
source: We traced and annotated all cells in a previously reported volume EM dataset of a 3-day-old (72 hours post fertilisation (hpf)) Platynereis larva (Randel et al., 2015; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The dataset consists of 4846 layers of 40 nm thin sections scanned by transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the dataset parameters and references the source data.

claim: 9162 cells with a soma were identified in the volume.
source: In the volume, we identified 9162 cells with a soma.
evidence: Direct statement of cell count from the reconstruction.

claim: The skeletons across the volume comprised 5,661,050 nodes and had 28,717 presynaptic and 27,538 postsynaptic sites.
source: The skeletons across the volume comprised 5,661,050 nodes and had 28,717 presynaptic and 27,538 postsynaptic sites.

claim: 15,020 fragments containing 896,428 nodes could not be attached to a skeleton with a soma.
source: We could not attach 15,020 fragments (896,428 nodes) to a skeleton with a soma.

claim: Overall, 15.8% of all nodes, 14.4% of presynaptic, and 19.3% of postsynaptic sites are on fragments and not assigned to a cell with a soma.
source: Overall, 15.8% of all nodes, 14.4% of presynaptic, and 19.3% of postsynaptic sites are on fragments and not assigned to a cell with a soma.
evidence: Calculated percentages from the reconstruction data.

claim: The Platynereis larval nervous system is subdivided into an anterior brain and a rope-ladder-like paired ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: The Platynereis larval nervous system is subdivided into an anterior brain and a rope-ladder-like paired ventral nerve cord (VNC).

claim: The brain and VNC are connected by circumesophageal connectives.
source: The brain and VNC are connected by circumesophageal connectives (Figure 1C and F–H).

claim: The trunk has five segments: an anterior cryptic segment (segment 0), three main segments (segments 1–3) with parapodia, and a posterior pygidium.
source: The trunk has five segments, an anterior cryptic segment (segment 0)(Saudemont et al., 2008; Steinmetz et al., 2011), three main segments (segments 1–3) with parapodia, and a posterior pygidium (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Anatomical description with citations and figure reference.

claim: Sensory neurons in the trunk only have ipsilateral projections that concentrate in two ventro-lateral bundles in the VNC.
source: Sensory neurons in the trunk only have ipsilateral projections that concentrate in two ventro-lateral bundles in the VNC (Figure 1I–K).

claim: Interneurons have either ipsi- or contralateral projections that remain in the VNC neuropil and also concentrate ventrally in the VNC.
source: Interneurons have either ipsi- or contralateral projections that remain in the VNC neuropil and also concentrate ventrally in the VNC (Figure 1K).

claim: Motoneurons can have ipsilateral and contralateral projections and are the only neuron class with peripheral afferent projections.
source: Motoneurons can have ipsilateral and contralateral projections and are the only neuron class with peripheral afferent projections (Figure 1J).

claim: Motor nerves concentrate dorsally in the VNC, close to the basal lamina and mesodermal muscles.
source: Motor nerves concentrate dorsally in the VNC (Figure 1K), close to the basal lamina and mesodermal muscles.

claim: Neurons have a median cable length of 97.1 µm (sensory neurons: 101.6 µm; interneurons: 87.77 µm, motoneurons: 139.8 µm).
source: Neurons have a median cable length of 97.1 µm (sensory neurons: 101.6 µm; interneurons: 87.77 µm, motoneurons: 139.8 µm) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Quantitative morphological data with figure reference.

claim: The largest neurons (Ser-tr1 and Loop) have a cable length of 1.2–1.7 mm.
source: the largest neurons (Ser-tr1 and Loop) have a cable length of 1.2–1.7 mm.

claim: Neurons have a median of eight presynaptic and six postsynaptic sites.
source: Neurons have a median of eight presynaptic and six postsynaptic sites with the largest neurons (MC, Ser-tr1, Loop) with over 300 presynapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative connectivity data with figure reference.

claim: The largest neurons (MC, Ser-tr1, Loop) have over 300 presynapses.
source: Neurons have a median of eight presynaptic and six postsynaptic sites with the largest neurons (MC, Ser-tr1, Loop) with over 300 presynapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative connectivity data with figure reference.

claim: The relative ratio of post- and presynaptic sites distinguishes sensory, inter-, and motoneurons, with sensory neurons having relatively more presynapses.
source: The relative ratio of post- and presynaptic sites distinguishes sensory, inter-, and motoneurons, with sensory neurons having relatively more presynapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Quantitative connectivity analysis with figure reference.

claim: The number of pre- and postsynaptic sites and skeleton segments scales with the total cable length of skeletons with Pearson's correlation coefficients >0.7.
source: The number of pre- and postsynaptic sites and skeleton segments scales with the total cable length of skeletons with Pearson's correlation coefficients >0.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–H).

claim: Most neuronal trees are unipolar and not highly branched (<100 segments).
source: Most neuronal trees are unipolar and not highly branched (<100 segments; Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).

claim: Neurons in general do not have primary cilia.
source: Neurons in general do not have primary cilia.

claim: Sensory neurons are bipolar with an axon and a sensory dendrite bearing zero to five sensory cilia at its distal tip, showing different sensory specialisations.
source: Sensory neurons are bipolar with an axon and a sensory dendrite bearing zero to five sensory cilia at its distal tip, showing different sensory specialisations (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2017).

claim: Interneurons are unipolar or pseudo-unipolar.
source: Interneurons are unipolar or pseudo-unipolar.

claim: Ciliomotor neurons have two motor axons emanating from the soma.
source: Ciliomotor neurons have two motor axons emanating from the soma (Verasztó et al., 2017)

claim: Other motoneurons are unipolar.
source: other motoneurons are unipolar.

claim: The final synaptic connectome contains 2675 nodes (including 467 fragments) connected by 14,066 directed edges formed by 26,881 in-graph synapses.
source: The final synaptic connectome contains 2675 nodes (including 467 fragments) connected by 14,066 directed edges formed by 26,881 in-graph synapses (Figure 2).
evidence: Quantitative network data with figure reference.

claim: The connectome is a sparsely connected network with a graph density of 0.00197.
source: The connectome is a sparsely connected network with a graph density of 0.00197.

claim: The majority of source nodes (nodes with only outgoing edges) are sensory neurons.
source: In the graph, the majority of source nodes (nodes with only outgoing edges) are sensory neurons

claim: Sink nodes (nodes with only incoming edges) are mostly effector cells.
source: sink nodes (nodes with only incoming edges) are mostly effector cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Network analysis result with figure reference.

claim: The nodes with the highest degree included ciliomotor neurons (e.g. Loop, Ser-tr1), the sensory-motoneuron pygPBunp, and the motoneurons of exocrine glands (MNspinning).
source: The nodes with the highest degree included ciliomotor neurons (e.g. Loop, Ser-tr1) (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Verasztó et al., 2017), the sensory-motoneuron pygPBunp (Verasztó et al., 2017), and the motoneurons of exocrine glands (MNspinning, see below).

claim: Some of the strongest edges (highest number of synapses) were between the pigment-cell motoneuron cioMNcover and prototroch pigment cells, MNspinning and exocrine glands, and the previously described MC cell and ciliated cells.
source: Some of the strongest edges (highest number of synapses) were between the pigment-cell motoneuron cioMNcover and prototroch pigment cells, MNspinning and exocrine glands, and the previously described MC cell and ciliated cells (Verasztó et al., 2017).

claim: Community detection with the Leiden algorithm combined with force-field-based clustering highlighted several modules in the connectome.
source: To identify more strongly connected subgraphs within the connectome, we used community detection with the Leiden algorithm (Traag et al., 2019). This analysis, combined with force-field-based clustering, highlighted several modules (Figure 2).
evidence: Network analysis method with citation and figure reference.

claim: Nodes in a module are more strongly interconnected than to nodes in other modules.
source: Nodes in a module are more strongly interconnected than to nodes in other modules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Network analysis result with figure reference.

claim: The modules include the anterior neurosecretory centre, the mushroom bodies, the visual circuit, a network of ciliomotor neurons, a module innervating head pigment cells, a left and right mechanosensory module providing input to muscles and segmental exocrine glands, a module for trunk postural control, and five muscle-motor modules.
source: The modules include the anterior neurosecretory centre, the mushroom bodies, the visual circuit, a network of ciliomotor neurons, a module innervating head pigment cells, a left and right mechanosensory module providing input to muscles and segmental exocrine glands, a module for trunk postural control, and five muscle-motor modules (Figure 2).
evidence: Network analysis result with figure reference.

claim: The visual module contains neurons of the eyes and primary visual neuropil (PRC, IN1, INint, INton) previously shown to mediate visual phototaxis.
source: The visual module contains neurons of the eyes and primary visual neuropil (PRC, IN1, INint, INton) previously shown to mediate visual phototaxis (Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: Module description with citation to functional study.

claim: The ciliomotor module contains ciliary band cells and functionally related neurons that show coordinated activity and drive ciliary closures and beating (Ser-tr1, Loop, MNant).
source: The ciliomotor module contains ciliary band cells and functionally related neurons that show coordinated activity and drive ciliary closures and beating (Ser-tr1, Loop, MNant) (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: Module description with citation to functional study.

claim: The anterior neurosecretory centre includes anterior and dorsal sensory neurons, the ciliary photoreceptors and their postsynaptic circuit, including the INRGWa and INNOS interneurons, as well as the Ser-h1 and MC ciliomotors with their prototroch targets.
source: The anterior neurosecretory centre includes anterior and dorsal sensory neurons, the ciliary photoreceptors and their postsynaptic circuit, including the INRGWa and INNOS interneurons, as well as the Ser-h1 and MC ciliomotors with their prototroch targets.

claim: Neurons in the anterior neurosecretory centre mediate barotaxis and UV avoidance.
source: Neurons in this module mediate barotaxis and UV avoidance (Calderón et al., 2023; Jokura et al., 2023; Verasztó et al., 2018).

claim: 966 neurons were classified into 202 cell types.
source: Based on these criteria, we classified 966 neurons into 202 cell types (Supplementary file 1, Video 1, Figure 3).
evidence: Cell classification result with supplementary file and figure references.

claim: Most neuronal cell types are represented by only two cells in the entire body.
source: Most neuronal cell types are represented by only two cells in the entire body (Figure 3D).
evidence: Cell type distribution with figure reference.

claim: 3128 non-neuronal cells were classified into 92 non-neuronal cell types.
source: Of these, 3128 were classified into 92 non-neuronal cell types (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell classification result with supplementary file and figure references.

claim: Non-neuronal cells included epidermal cells (1334 cells), various pigment cells (158 cells of seven types), muscle cells (853 cells of 53 types), locomotor ciliated cells (80 cells of six types), glial cells (78 cells of three types), gland cells (54 cells of six types), various support and sheet cells, nephridia, putative migratory cells, parapodial cells producing chitin chaetae (106 cells) or aciculae (12 cells), and the follicle cells (566 cells of five types) ensheathing them.
source: These included epidermal cells (1334 cells), various pigment cells (158 cells of seven types), muscle cells (853 cells of 53 types, described in Jasek et al., 2022), locomotor ciliated cells (80 cells of six types, described in Verasztó et al., 2017), glial cells (78 cells of three types), gland cells (54 cells of six types), various support and sheet cells, nephridia, putative migratory cells, parapodial cells producing chitin chaetae (106 cells) or aciculae (12 cells), and the follicle cells (566 cells of five types) ensheathing them (Supplementary file 1; Video 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell classification result with citations and supplementary file references.

claim: The developing antennae contain 115 cells of which the majority have only a few or no synapses and immature sensory dendrites.
source: The developing antennae contain 115 cells of which the majority have only a few or no synapses and immature sensory dendrites.
evidence: Cell count and developmental state description.

claim: In the developing palps, 82 developing sensory neurons were found.
source: In the developing palps, we found 82 developing sensory neurons.

claim: The developing mouth or stomodeum (675 cells) is lined with 52 immature sensory neurons.
source: The developing mouth or stomodeum (675 cells) is lined with 52 immature sensory neurons.

claim: The cell-type connectome included 84 sensory, 82 interneurons, 34 motoneuron types, and 58 effector cell types (including ciliary band, muscle, gland, and pigmented cell types).
source: This cell-type connectome included 84 sensory, 82 interneurons, 34 motoneuron types, and 58 effector cell types (including ciliary band, muscle, gland, and pigmented cell types) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell type count with figure reference.

claim: The cell-type graph had 2410 edges formed by 14,640 synapses.
source: The cell-type graph had 2410 edges formed by 14,640 synapses (Figure 4).

claim: The correlation of the left and right synapse matrices was 0.91, indicating a high level of stereotypy of connectivity.
source: The correlation of the left and right synapse matrices was 0.91, indicating a high level of stereotypy of connectivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: The cell-type graph is characterised by network parameters similar to the C. elegans and C. intestinalis connectome graphs.
source: The cell-type graph is characterised by network parameters similar to the C. elegans and C. intestinalis connectome graphs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Comparative network analysis with figure reference.

claim: Four sensory neurons with direct motor output were identified (sensory-motor neurons: eyespot-PRCR3, pygPBunp, pygCirrusPUSM, hPU2l-asymPDF).
source: We identified four sensory neurons with direct motor output (sensory-motor neurons: eyespot-PRCR3, pygPBunp, pygCirrusPUSM, hPU2l-asymPDF)

claim: 25 premotor sensory neurons were identified.
source: and 25 premotor sensory neurons.

claim: The maximum number of hops from sensory neurons to an effector is five.
source: The maximum number of hops from sensory neurons to an effector is five.

claim: 33 sensory neurons have no synaptic paths to effectors.
source: 33 sensory neurons have no synaptic paths to effectors.

claim: 19 of the sensory neurons with no synaptic paths to effectors are neurosecretory cells with few or no synaptic partners.
source: 19 of these are neurosecretory cells with few or no synaptic partners (Williams et al., 2017; Table 1).

claim: Neurotransmitters or neuropeptides could be assigned to 53 (26%) neuronal cell types.
source: We could assign neurotransmitters or neuropeptides to 53 (26%) neuronal cell types (Figure 5).
evidence: Molecular characterization result with figure reference.

claim: 11 cholinergic, three serotonergic, one dopaminergic, one adrenergic, and four glutamatergic neuronal cell types were annotated.
source: We annotated 11 cholinergic, three serotonergic, one dopaminergic, one adrenergic, and four glutamatergic neuronal cell types.

claim: One of 12 neuropeptides was assigned to 38 cell types (pigment dispersing factor — 12, allatotropin/orexin — 5, leucokinin — 1, proenkephalin — 1, FVamide — 5, FMRFamide — 3, myoinhibitory peptide — 3, achatin — 1, RGWamide — 1, MLD/pedal peptide — 1, IRP2 — 1, WLD — 1).
source: In addition, we assigned one of 12 neuropeptides to 38 cell types (pigment dispersing factor — 12, allatotropin/orexin — 5, leucokinin — 1, proenkephalin — 1, FVamide — 5, FMRFamide — 3, myoinhibitory peptide — 3, achatin — 1, RGWamide — 1, MLD/pedal peptide — 1, IRP2 — 1, WLD — 1).

claim: 516 connectome neurons contained dense core vesicles, indicative of peptidergic transmission.
source: In agreement with the large number of neuropeptides expressed in the larva (Conzelmann et al., 2011; Shahidi et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017), 516 connectome neurons contained dense core vesicles, indicative of peptidergic transmission (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Ultrastructural observation with citations and figure reference.

claim: The head contains 45 sensory neuron types with postsynaptic partners, including 52 head interneuron types directly postsynaptic to sensory neurons.
source: The head contains 45 sensory neuron types with postsynaptic partners, including 52 head interneuron types directly postsynaptic to sensory neurons (Figure 3).
evidence: Cell type count with figure reference.

claim: Information flows from various sensory neuron clusters to head interneurons that converge on ciliomotor, head ventral motoneuron (vMNs), and head descending interneuron groups.
source: Information flows from various sensory neuron clusters to head interneurons that converge on ciliomotor, head ventral motoneuron (vMNs), and head descending interneuron groups (Figure 6H).

claim: There is recurrent connectivity between some interneuron clusters (e.g. between INMBintr and INcentrHead) and within-cluster connectivity (e.g. visualIN, INcentralHead).
source: There is recurrent connectivity between some interneuron clusters (e.g. between INMBintr and INcentrHead) and within-cluster connectivity (e.g. visualIN, INcentralHead).

claim: Three pairs of ventral head motoneurons (the vMNs: MN1, MN2, MN3) are at the core of a postural control module.
source: One direct motor output of head circuits are three pairs of ventral head motoneurons (the vMNs: MN1, MN2, MN3) (Randel et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014). These decussating (crossing the midline before descending) motoneurons are at the core of a postural control module (Figure 2; Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Circuit description with citations and figure references.

claim: The vMNs have a decussating morphology and innervate contralateral ciliated cells and ventral and dorsal longitudinal muscles, controlling trunk bending and the laterality of ciliary beating.
source: The vMNs have a decussating morphology and innervate contralateral ciliated cells and ventral and dorsal longitudinal muscles, controlling trunk bending and the laterality of ciliary beating (Randel et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014).
evidence: Anatomical and functional description with citations.

claim: Two types of exocrine glands in the first segment (ciliated gland, MVgland) are innervated by two MNgland-head gland-motor neurons.
source: Another motor output from the head is two types of exocrine glands in the first segment (ciliated gland, MVgland). These are innervated by two MNgland-head gland-motor neurons.

claim: The MNgland-head cells receive input from the rhythmically active serotonergic Ser-h1 ciliomotor neurons, suggesting a link between ciliary activity and glandular secretion.
source: The MNgland-head cells receive input from the rhythmically active serotonergic Ser-h1 ciliomotor neurons (Verasztó et al., 2017), suggesting a link between ciliary activity and glandular secretion.
evidence: Circuit analysis with citation and functional inference.

claim: Several head ciliomotor neurons directly innervate locomotor ciliary bands (MC, Ser-h1, MNant, vMN).
source: Furthermore, several head ciliomotor neurons directly innervate locomotor ciliary bands (Verasztó et al., 2017) (MC, Ser-h1, MNant, vMN).

claim: The MNant cells receive direct input from several head sensory neurons (SNhook, SNtorii, SNantler, SNhorn).
source: Of these, the MNant cells receive direct input from several head sensory neurons (SNhook, SNtorii, SNantler, SNhorn) (Figure 7F).

claim: The visual eye photoreceptors (PRC) share a postsynaptic interneuron (INR) with the PRCR1 photoreceptors of the eyespots.
source: Here, the visual eye photoreceptors (PRC) share a postsynaptic interneuron (INR) with the PRCR1 photoreceptors of the eyespots (Figure 7G and H).

claim: The MNant and vMN motoneurons have among the highest number of presynaptic partners.
source: The MNant and vMN motoneurons have among the highest number of presynaptic partners.

claim: Among the interneurons, INRGW, INarc1, and INW integrate the largest number of inputs.
source: Among the interneurons, INRGW, INarc1, and INW integrate the largest number of inputs.

claim: The head collar receptor neurons (hCR) that mediate a startle response have the largest number of postsynaptic cell types.
source: Regarding the multiplicity of outputs, the head collar receptor neurons (hCR) that mediate a startle response (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) stand out with the largest number of postsynaptic cell types.
evidence: Network analysis result with citation to functional study.

claim: The mushroom bodies (MBs) are formed by a pair of ventrolateral brain ganglia comprising both sensory and interneurons (SNMB and INMB).
source: The mushroom bodies (MBs) are formed by a pair of ventrolateral brain ganglia. They comprise both sensory and interneurons (SNMB and INMB) (Figure 8A–D).

claim: Most SNMB cells project to two lateral MB neuropils and a few to the anterior neurosecretory plexus.
source: Most SNMB cells project to two lateral MB neuropils and a few to the anterior neurosecretory plexus (Figure 8B), in agreement with the projection reconstructions (Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: Anatomical description with figure reference and citation.

claim: INMBs were classified into intrinsic (MBintrIN) and output projection (MBON) types.
source: We classified INMBs into intrinsic (MBintrIN) and output projection (MBON) types (Figure 8C and D).

claim: MBintrINs project to the MB neuropils, MBONs project ventrally to the VNC or to the developing mouth (stomodeum).
source: MBintrINs project to the MB neuropils, MBONs project ventrally to the VNC or to the developing mouth (stomodeum) (Figure 8C–G; Video 3).
evidence: Anatomical description with figure and video references.

claim: Besides MB-intrinsic sensory neurons, MBs receive sensory input from the antennae, the palps, and two further sensory neuron types (SNbronto, SNstiff).
source: Besides MB-intrinsic sensory neurons, MBs receive sensory input from the antennae, the palps, and two further sensory neuron types (SNbronto, SNstiff) (Figure 9A–D).

claim: There is cell-type-specific connectivity between sensory neuron types and interneurons, with groups organised into specific micro-circuits.
source: There is cell-type-specific connectivity between sensory neuron types and interneurons, with groups organised into specific micro-circuits (Figure 9B, E–G, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: The morphology and connectivity of distinct mushroom body cell types shows left-right symmetry.
source: The morphology and connectivity of distinct mushroom body cell types shows left-right symmetry. The Sholl diagrams are similar for left-right pairs and the correlation coefficient of the left and right connectivity matrices is 0.76 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Morphological and connectivity analysis with figure reference.

claim: The correlation coefficient of the left and right connectivity matrices for mushroom body cell types is 0.76.
source: The Sholl diagrams are similar for left-right pairs and the correlation coefficient of the left and right connectivity matrices is 0.76 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).

claim: The overall architecture of the Platynereis MB is multilayer, parallel, and feed-forward, with only very weak recurrent connections or lateral connections between the feed-forward networks.
source: The overall architecture of the Platynereis MB is multilayer, parallel, and feed-forward, with only very weak recurrent connections or lateral connections between the feed-forward networks (Figure 9B; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Circuit architecture analysis with figure references.

claim: The circuit shows a fan-out fan-in architecture, with the sensory neurons diverging to several IN targets and post-MB interneurons receiving converging input.
source: The circuit also shows a fan-out fan-in architecture, with the sensory neurons diverging to several IN targets (e.g. SNtorii to INtorii, INbigloop, and INhorn) and post-MB interneurons receiving converging input (e.g. INW from INhook, INlasso, INMBtype5-6, and SNlasso).

claim: This multilayer perceptron architecture may support the formation of associative memories, as proposed for memory circuits in cephalopods.
source: This multilayer perceptron architecture may support the formation of associative memories, as proposed for memory circuits in cephalopods (Shomrat et al., 2011).
evidence: Functional speculation with citation to comparative study.

claim: There are 138 brain neurons that descend to the VNC and 75 VNC neurons that ascend to the brain.
source: There are 138 brain neurons that descend to the VNC and 75 VNC neurons that ascend to the brain (Figure 10C and D).

claim: There are 549 trunk connectome cells that receive synapses from head neurons and 288 head connectome cells that receive synapses from trunk neurons.
source: There are 549 trunk connectome cells that receive synapses from head neurons and 288 head connectome cells that receive synapses from trunk neurons (Figure 10E and G).

claim: The trunk-projecting brain neurons have either a decussating or ipsilaterally descending morphology.
source: The trunk-projecting brain neurons have either a decussating or ipsilaterally descending morphology.

claim: The two types of trunk-projecting brain neurons project to different domains of the VNC and have different target neurons.
source: The two types project to different domains of the VNC and have different target neurons (Figure 10—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Anatomical and connectivity analysis with figure reference.

claim: Decussating and descending neurons receive most of their synaptic inputs (postsynaptic sites) in the central head neuropil and form most of their presynapses in the VNC.
source: Decussating and descending neurons receive most of their synaptic inputs (postsynaptic sites) in the central head neuropil and form most of their presynapses in the VNC (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C, D, H–M).

claim: The 3-day-old larva has three main trunk segments with chaeta-bearing parapodia (chaetigerous segments) and a more anterior cryptic segment.
source: The 3-day-old larva has three main trunk segments with chaeta-bearing parapodia (chaetigerous segments) and a more anterior cryptic segment (Saudemont et al., 2008; Steinmetz et al., 2011).

claim: The pygidium forms the posterior-most part of the body.
source: In addition, the pygidium forms the posterior-most part of the body (Starunov et al., 2015; Figures 1A and 11A).
evidence: Anatomical description with citation and figure reference.

claim: The ciliary bands mark the posterior segment boundaries.
source: The ciliary bands mark the posterior segment boundaries.

claim: The strongest connections are formed within segments, but there are also connections between any pair of segments with the exception of segment 0.
source: Breaking down connections to segments (head, sg0-3, pygidium) or to cell classes (SN, IN, MN, effector) and segments shows that the strongest connections are formed within segments, but there are also connections between any pair of segments with the exception of segment 0 (Figure 11B–D, F and G; Figure 11—figure supplement 1).

claim: Segment 1 interneurons connect to cells in four other body regions.
source: Segment 1 interneurons, for example, connect to cells in four other body regions (Figure 11G).

claim: The head, segment 1, and the pygidium all contain neurons that project along the entire length of the body (neurons with 'global reach').
source: The head, segment 1, and the pygidium all contain neurons that project along the entire length of the body (neurons with 'global reach')(Figure 11L–N).

claim: Ciliary band cells receive most of their innervation from the head and first segment.
source: Ciliary band cells receive most of their innervation from the head and first segment (Figure 11E).

claim: Gland cells receive most of their synapses from the second segment.
source: Gland cells receive most of their synapses from the second segment.

claim: Muscles are innervated by motoneurons with somas in the head and segments 1–3.
source: Muscles are innervated by motoneurons with somas in the head and segments 1–3.

claim: Pigment cells receive their inputs predominantly from pygidial neurons.
source: In contrast, pigment cells receive their inputs predominantly from pygidial neurons (Figure 11E).

claim: There are 10 neuronal cell types specific to the first segment, eight to the second segment, two to the third segment, and seven to the pygidium.
source: There are 10 neuronal cell types specific to the first segment, eight to the second segment, two to the third segment, and seven to the pygidium (Figure 12, Figure 12—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Cell type distribution with figure references.

claim: The first segment contains ciliomotor neurons involved in body-wide ciliary closures and beating.
source: The first segment contains ciliomotor neurons involved in body-wide ciliary closures and beating (Figure 12; Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: Functional description with citation and figure reference.

claim: Segment 2 contains a unique pair of giant motoneurons (MNspinning) that extensively innervate the contralateral spinning glands (spinGland) in the second and third segments.
source: Segment 2 contains a unique pair of giant motoneurons (MNspinning) that extensively innervate the contralateral spinning glands (spinGland) in the second and third segments (Figure 12E and F).
evidence: Anatomical and connectivity description with figure reference.

claim: The four spinGland cells have a large microvillar secretory pore at the tip of the ventral parapodia (neuropodia).
source: The four spinGland cells have a large microvillar secretory pore at the tip of the ventral parapodia (neuropodia).

claim: MNspinning cells form reciprocal connections with pseudounipolar INsplit mechanosensory interneurons.
source: MNspinning cells form reciprocal connections with pseudounipolar INsplit mechanosensory interneurons (Figure 12I).

claim: Segment 2 also contains the large contra- and ipsilaterally projecting MNbow motoneurons and four types of unique interneurons.
source: Segment 2 also contains the large contra- and ipsilaterally projecting MNbow motoneurons and four types of unique interneurons (Figure 12G and H).

claim: The cioMNcover and pygPBunp motoneurons innervate the head cover cells (with large pigment vacuoles) that occur in two rings anterior and posterior to the head protoroch ciliary band.
source: The cioMNcover and pygPBunp motoneurons innervate the head cover cells (with large pigment vacuoles) that occur in two rings anterior and posterior to the head protoroch ciliary band (Figure 12J and K).
evidence: Connectivity and anatomical description with figure reference.

claim: The pygPBunp neuron also synapses on another head pigmented cell type (vacuolar cell).
source: The pygPBunp neuron also synapses on another head pigmented cell type (vacuolar cell).

claim: Several neuron types occur in all chaetigerous segments, including the chaeMech sensory neurons, the INsplitPB and INbackcross interneurons and the MNche and MNhose motoneurons.
source: At the same time, several neuron types occur in all chaetigerous segments. These include the chaeMech sensory neurons (Figure 15A), the INsplitPB (Figure 16B), and INbackcross interneurons and the MNche and MNhose motoneurons (not shown).
evidence: Cell type distribution with figure references.

claim: Four cell-type families (CR, PU, PB, INsplit) and two muscle types (MUSlongV, MUStrans) occur across five or six body regions (head, segments 0–3, and pygidium).
source: Four cell-type families (CR, PU, PB, INsplit) and two muscle types (MUSlongV, MUStrans) occur across five or six body regions (head, segments 0–3, and pygidium) (Figure 13).
evidence: Cell type distribution with figure reference.

claim: This pattern may indicate serial homology, suggesting a metameric evolutionary origin for the trunk segments, the pygidium, and the head.
source: This pattern may indicate serial homology, suggesting a metameric evolutionary origin for the trunk segments, the pygidium, and the head.
evidence: Evolutionary inference from cell type distribution.

claim: The mechanosensory neurons and their postsynaptic partners form an anatomically distinct system that spans the entire body of the larva, termed the mechanosensory girdle.
source: The mechanosensory neurons and their postsynaptic partners form an anatomically distinct system that spans the entire body of the larva. Based on its morphology with a circumoral ring that continues in two VNC tracts, we termed this system the mechanosensory girdle (Figure 14; Figure 14—figure supplement 1; Video 4).
evidence: Anatomical description with figure and video references.

claim: The girdle includes the penetrating vibration-sensing collar receptor (CR) neurons, the penetrating biciliated (PB) neurons, the penetrating uniciliated (PU) neurons, the interparapodial penetrating multiciliated (interparaPM) neurons.
source: The girdle includes the penetrating vibration-sensing collar receptor (CR) neurons (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018), the penetrating biciliated (PB) neurons, the penetrating uniciliated (PU) neurons, the interparapodial penetrating multiciliated (interparaPM) neurons (Video 5).
evidence: Anatomical description with citation and video reference.

claim: These penetrating cells all have one or more penetrating sensory cilia surrounded by a collar of microvilli.
source: These penetrating cells all have one or more penetrating sensory cilia surrounded by a collar of microvilli.

claim: The CR and PB neurons express the mechanosensory polycystin PKD2-1, with CRs also expressing PKD1-1.
source: The CR and PB neurons express the mechanosensory polycystin PKD2-1, with CRs also expressing PKD1-1 (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).

claim: The girdle also includes the chaeMech dendritic cells that are chaetal mechanoreceptors.
source: The girdle also includes the chaeMech dendritic cells that are chaetal mechanoreceptors (Figure 15 and see below).
evidence: Cell type description with figure reference.

claim: The chaeMechs are dendritic sensory cells in segments 1–3 in both the dorsal (notopodium) and the ventral (neuropodium) lobes of the parapodia.
source: The chaeMechs are part of the mechanosensory girdle and are dendritic sensory cells in segments 1–3 in both the dorsal (notopodium) and the ventral (neuropodium) lobes of the parapodia (Video 5).

claim: The sensory dendrites of chaeMech cells branch between the chaetal sacs and may sense the displacement of the chaetae during crawling (proprioception) or due to external mechanical stimuli.
source: The sensory dendrites of chaeMech cells branch between the chaetal sacs (Figure 15A–D) and may sense the displacement of the chaetae during crawling (proprioception) or due to external mechanical stimuli.
evidence: Anatomical observation with figure reference and functional speculation.

claim: The annelids Harmothoë (a polynoid) and Nereis (a nereid) have cells with a similar morphology called bristle receptors that show rapidly adapting spikes upon the displacement of the chaetae.
source: The annelids Harmothoë (a polynoid) and Nereis (a nereid) have cells with a similar morphology called bristle receptors. These cells show rapidly adapting spikes upon the displacement of the chaetae (Dorsett, 1964; Horridge, 1963).

claim: The chaeMech cells are reminiscent of dendritic proprioceptors in Drosophila larvae that sense body-wall deformations and provide feedback about body position through premotor neurons.
source: The chaeMech cells are also reminiscent of dendritic proprioceptors in Drosophila larvae that sense body-wall deformations and provide feedback about body position through premotor neurons (He et al., 2019; Vaadia et al., 2019; Zarin et al., 2019).

claim: In Harmothoë and Nereis, the bristle receptors connect to the giant axon system.
source: In Harmothoë and Nereis, the bristle receptors connect to the giant axon system.

claim: In Platynereis, chaeMech neurons are highly interconnected and project into the VNC where inputs and outputs are mixed on the chaeMech axons.
source: In Platynereis, chaeMech neurons are highly interconnected. They project into the VNC where inputs and outputs are mixed on the chaeMech axons (Figure 15B).

claim: The direct postsynaptic partners of chaeMech cells include the premotor interneurons INsplitCR, INsplitBronto, INchaeMech, and the MNring and MNspinning motoneurons.
source: The direct postsynaptic partners of chaeMech cells include the premotor interneurons INsplitCR, INsplitBronto, INchaeMech, and the MNring and MNspinning motoneurons (Figure 15E and F).

claim: The innervation of MNspinning by chaeMech (and also indirectly by PB mechanosensory neurons) suggests that parapodial mechanosensation may regulate glandular secretion of the spinGlands.
source: The innervation of MNspinning by chaeMech (and also indirectly by PB mechanosensory neurons; Figure 12I) suggests that parapodial mechanosensation may regulate glandular secretion of the spinGlands.
evidence: Connectivity analysis with figure reference and functional inference.

claim: Among the direct targets of chaeMech neurons, the INsplitCR interneurons receive the largest number of chaeMech synapses.
source: Among the direct targets of chaeMech neurons, the INsplitCR interneurons receive the largest number of chaeMech synapses (Figure 15E).

claim: INsplitCR interneurons are postsynaptic to the collar receptors (CR) that mediate a hydrodynamic startle response characterised by parapodial elevation and the extension of the chaetae.
source: These neurons are also postsynaptic to the collar receptors (CR) that mediate a hydrodynamic startle response characterised by parapodial elevation and the extension of the chaetae (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
evidence: Connectivity and functional description with citation.

claim: chaeMech do not or only weakly synapse on INrope and INCM neurons, which are one of the main targets of CRs.
source: At the same time, chaeMech do not or only weakly synapse on INrope and INCM neurons, which are one of the main targets of CRs

claim: INchaeMech neurons lack synaptic inputs from CRs.
source: and INchaeMech neurons lack synaptic inputs from CRs.

claim: The postsynaptic circuits of CRs and chaeMechs are only partially overlapping.
source: This shows that the postsynaptic circuits of CRs and chaeMechs are only partially overlapping.

claim: The shared innervation of INsplitCR by CRs and chaeMechs suggests that there may be proprioceptive inhibitory feedback during the startle response provided by chaeMechs through the INsplitCR cells.
source: The shared innervation of INsplitCR by CRs and chaeMechs suggests that there may be proprioceptive inhibitory feedback during the startle response provided by chaeMechs through the INsplitCR cells.

claim: The strongest postsynaptic partners of the diverse girdle mechanosensory neurons are ipsilateral interneurons with a bifurcating projection (presudounipolar morphology), collectively referred to as INsplit.
source: The strongest postsynaptic partners of the diverse girdle mechanosensory neurons are ipsilateral interneurons with a bifurcating projection (presudounipolar morphology). This family of interneurons — collectively referred to as INsplit — could be subdivided into several distinct cell types (INsplitCR, INsplitPB, INsplitPBant, INsplitPB-RF/Ya, INsplitPUh, INsplitBronto, INCM)(Figure 16A–H; Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
evidence: Connectivity and morphological analysis with figure reference and citation.

claim: INsplit neurons occur in all four trunk segments and in the head (INsplitPUh) and the distinct types have unique synaptic connectivity.
source: INsplit neurons occur in all four trunk segments and in the head (INsplitPUh) and the distinct types have unique synaptic connectivity.
evidence: Cell type distribution and connectivity analysis.

claim: PB and interparaPM neurons specifically target INsplitPB and represent their main input.
source: PB and interparaPM neurons specifically target INsplitPB and represent their main input (Figure 16B and E).

claim: SNbronto and chaeMech neurons both synapse on the INsplitBronto interneurons, which have no other major presynaptic partners.
source: SNbronto and chaeMech neurons both synapse on the INsplitBronto interneurons (Figures 15E, F, 16C), which have no other major presynaptic partners.

claim: CR and chaeMech neurons synapse on INsplitCR while CR neurons also target INCM.
source: CR and chaeMech neurons synapse on INsplitCR (Figure 16A) while CR neurons also target INCM (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
evidence: Connectivity analysis with figure reference and citation.

claim: Some head PU neurons synapse on INsplitPUh.
source: Some head PU neurons synapse on INsplitPUh (Figure 16D).

claim: Among trunk neuron types, INsplitCR and INsplitPB cells are highly ranked based on the number of pre- and postsynaptic partners, suggesting an integrating function.
source: Among trunk neuron types, INsplitCR and INsplitPB cells are highly ranked based on the number of pre- and postsynaptic partners, suggesting an integrating function (Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Network analysis with figure reference and functional inference.

claim: INsplit neurons are premotor neurons, with connections to several trunk motoneuron types that in turn innervate glands, ciliated cells, muscles, and pigment cells.
source: INsplit neurons are premotor neurons, with connections to several trunk motoneuron types that in turn innervate glands, ciliated cells, muscles, and pigment cells (Figure 16I, Figure 16—figure supplement 1).

claim: Mechanosensory neurons provide input to all effector systems in the body.
source: Mechanosensory neurons thus provide input to all effector systems in the body.
